case.name: The Buzzword Hand-Wave (Fatal GTM Mismatch)
case.idea: Decentralized AI Quantum Matching Engine for Gen-Z commercial real estate leases with zero sales team and 100% viral word-of-mouth adoption.
case.expected_failure_mode: Ungrounded viral assumption; zero CAC in enterprise sales.

evidence_voids: Quantified customer acquisition cost (CAC) for a purely word‑of‑mouth launch.
Projected viral adoption metrics (K‑factor, referral conversion) for Gen‑Z leasing.
Unit economics: average lease size, gross margin, operating expense, LTV for the decentralized platform.
Regulatory analysis of blockchain/smart‑contract lease execution across key jurisdictions (US, EU, Singapore, APAC).
Empirical validation of any quantum‑computing advantage in property‑matching algorithms.
TAM/SAM/SOM for Gen‑Z commercial real‑estate leasing specifically (square footage, spend, growth rate).
Competitor financial or adoption benchmarks for AI‑driven matching engines (e.g., Dazzle.ai, VentionTeams).
Minimum network‑effect threshold (active users needed) to generate reliable matches.
offline_experiments: Run a controlled pilot with a representative Gen‑Z cohort to measure willingness to adopt a decentralized AI lease matching tool and capture referral K‑factor.
Commission a legal feasibility study with real‑estate lawyers in Singapore, the US, and the EU to map compliance gaps for smart‑contract lease execution.
Develop a minimal viable quantum‑enhanced matching prototype and benchmark latency/cost against classical AI models on real listing data.
adaptive.audit_critique: The dossier is a collage of macro CRE headlines and generic AI adoption stats that never touch the core venture hypotheses. No hard numbers on CAC, LTV, viral K‑factor, quantum advantage, or Gen‑Z specific lease demand. Regulators, smart‑contract legality, and unit economics are glossed over. Contradictory signals (high AI anxiety vs 100% viral adoption; office‑centric recovery vs a co‑living focus) are ignored. Evidence is superficial and region‑agnostic despite a global rollout claim.

case.name: The Contradictory Regulatory Market
case.idea: Cross-border algorithmic remittance and instant debit card platform between Trinidad & Tobago and the US bypassing commercial bank FX queues.
case.expected_failure_mode: Strict Central Bank Exchange Control regulations contradict open crypto access claims.

evidence_voids: No quantitative estimate of annual US‑to‑Trinidad & Tobago remittance volume or diaspora size.
No source or calculation supporting the claim that the platform can deliver <5% total cost.
No data on current FX processing times or queue lengths for banks in Trinidad & Tobago.
Absence of regulatory framework details for a non‑bank entity to bypass commercial‑bank FX queues.
No cost breakdown for building/operating an algorithmic cross‑border FX engine in the Caribbean context.
No evidence on debit‑card issuance rules, costs, or adoption rates in Trinidad & Tobago.
Missing unit‑economic assumptions (CAC, LTV, gross margin) for the proposed business model.
Reliance on global cost benchmarks (banks 12%, MTOs 5.5%) without Caribbean‑specific validation.
offline_experiments: Run a controlled pilot with a small cohort of US‑based senders (n≈30) to measure actual cost, latency, and settlement success when routing through a prototype algorithmic FX layer.

Conduct in‑depth interviews with at least five officials from the Central Bank of Trinidad and Tobago and the Financial Services Commission to map the legal pathway and potential barriers for a non‑bank FX broker.
Survey a minimum of 150 TT‑based recipients to assess willingness to adopt an instant debit card linked to remittance inflows and to gauge trust thresholds.
adaptive.audit_critique: The package strings together high‑level regional trends and generic cost benchmarks but fails to substantiate the core venture hypotheses with Caribbean‑specific data. Critical assumptions—US‑TT remittance volume, diaspora size, current FX queue latency, licensing path for a non‑bank FX broker, and cost structure of an algorithmic platform—are asserted without quantitative backing. Global cost percentages are transplanted onto a market that may have very different fee regimes and regulatory friction. Contradictory signals around FX liquidity (tight market vs. Central Bank's liquidity guarantee) and regulatory readiness are mentioned but never reconciled. Overall the evidence is thin, regionally mismatched, and leans on founder optimism rather than verifiable metrics.

case.name: The Obscure Regional Niche (Data Deficit)
case.idea: Industrial LoRaWAN sub-surface cold storage sensors for indigenous soursop and seamoss cooperative farming in Dominica.
case.expected_failure_mode: Near-zero public web pricing/infrastructure data; requires physical grower validation.

evidence_voids: No quantitative estimate of LoRaWAN coverage, latency, or subscription cost in Dominica's rural/co‑operative zones.
Absence of unit‑economic breakdown for the sensor hardware (CAPEX, OPEX, battery life, maintenance) and its impact on cooperative margins.
Missing data on the volume and value of Dominican soursop and sea‑moss production, and the price premium achievable through traceability.
No citation of Dominica's export licensing, phytosanitary requirements, or specific duty rates for sea‑moss under CARICOM CET.
Lack of benchmark for customer acquisition cost (CAC) for a B2B cooperative sales model in the Caribbean.
No evidence of consumer willingness‑to‑pay for “premium, traceable” sea‑moss from Caribbean buyers versus established Asian suppliers.
offline_experiments: Deploy a pilot LoRaWAN sensor suite in at least two cooperative cold‑storage sites in Dominica for 3‑months to capture temperature stability, battery life, and data transmission reliability.

Conduct a buyer interview series with at least five premium health‑food distributors in the US/North America to quantify the price premium they would pay for traceable, Caribbean‑sourced sea moss with sensor‑verified quality.
adaptive.audit_critique: The package leans heavily on global sea‑moss market numbers and generic Caribbean FMCG trends while offering no hard data on the core hardware proposition, local cooperative economics, or regulatory specifics for Dominica exports. Sensor cost, LoRaWAN network availability, and the financial impact of the quoted import duties are all asserted without quantitative anchors. Regional mismatches abound – Asian market share is cited to justify demand, yet no Caribbean‑specific demand or pricing data for soursop or sea‑moss is provided. Contradictory duty information (220% max vs. 5‑35% average) is left unresolved. Overall, the evidence is insufficient to confirm key venture hypotheses.

case.name: The Grounded B2B SaaS (Established Market)
case.idea: Shopify plugin for automated VAT calculation and tax authority compliant e-invoicing for regional Caribbean eCommerce merchants.
case.expected_failure_mode: None; known market with clear public benchmarks.

evidence_voids: Exact number of active Shopify merchants (and Shopify Plus stores) operating in each Caribbean jurisdiction.
Quantified size of Caribbean e‑commerce sales (GMV) relevant to VAT compliance tooling revenue potential.
Detailed, jurisdiction‑specific VAT rates, filing frequencies, e‑invoicing legal requirements, and any mandatory integration standards.
Demonstrated merchant willingness to pay (price sensitivity) and expected CAC/LTV for a tax‑automation plugin.
Competitor coverage matrix showing which existing accounting/invoicing tools support (or fail to support) each Caribbean country's tax rules.
Projected unit economics (margin assumptions, expected support costs for regulatory updates).
offline_experiments: Conduct structured interviews or surveys with a representative sample of Caribbean Shopify merchants to quantify pain points, current manual compliance costs, and price willingness for an automated VAT/e‑invoicing solution.
Run a limited‑pilot deployment of the plugin with 5‑10 merchants across different Caribbean jurisdictions to collect real usage data, CAC, churn, and compliance outcome metrics.
adaptive.audit_critique: The dossier leans heavily on global Shopify metrics and generic Caribbean e‑commerce observations while omitting any hard numbers on the actual addressable market, merchant pain‑points, regulatory specifics, and unit economics. Claims of a "critical gap" and "high‑volume" Caribbean Shopify merchants are unsupported, and the data cited often conflicts (e.g., citing precise revenue shares despite stating statistical offices lack data). Regional regulatory nuance is assumed from global trends, creating a substantial evidentiary void and sycophantic validation of the founder's thesis.

case.name: The Unverifiable Consumer Habit
case.idea: Social peer accountability app where friends lock up cash deposits that are forfeited if they miss their daily 8-glass water drinking goal.
case.expected_failure_mode: Web search only reveals generic wellness TAM; cannot validate novel behavioral willingness to stake cash.

evidence_voids: Absence of any quantified total addressable market (TAM) for hydration‑tracking or accountability apps worldwide or for Trinidad & Tobago specifically.
No data on average user willingness to lock up cash deposits for health goals, nor typical deposit amounts or conversion rates.
Missing CAC / CPA benchmarks for peer‑to‑peer health apps; no cost‑per‑install or funnel metrics.
No citation of legal/regulatory frameworks governing escrowed funds, forfeiture penalties, or consumer‑protection constraints in the target jurisdictions.
Lack of any pricing, unit‑economic, or margin model (e.g., subscription fee, transaction fee, operating costs).
No competitor usage statistics (DAU/MAU) to substantiate the claim that existing habit‑trackers lack financial accountability.
No evidence that smart‑water‑bottle integrations or utility‑data APIs are available or adoptable in the cited regions.
No global or regional data on smartphone penetration, internet connectivity, or app store adoption rates beyond a vague statement.
offline_experiments: Conduct a small‑scale user pilot (n≥100) in Port of Spain to measure deposit willingness, default rates, and churn under real financial penalties.
Run a legal feasibility workshop with a Caribbean financial‑services regulator to validate escrow and forfeiture mechanisms.
adaptive.audit_critique: The dossier is a collage of isolated health statistics for Trinidad & Tobago, with no quantitative grounding for the core venture assumptions (market size, CAC, deposit size, legal feasibility, global demand). It cherry‑picks macro health trends, ignores contradictory signals (water scarcity both drives and thwarts hydration incentives), and substitutes regional data for a claimed global market. Founder‑centric assertions about peer‑financial accountability are never validated by independent usage or financial‑services benchmarks.
